newsitem.title: ITALY: Head of Italy's Somalia probe seeks strong powers.
newsitem.headline: Head of Italy's Somalia probe seeks strong powers.

text.p: A respected judge, named by Italy's government to head an urgent inquiry into allegations that troops in Somalia indulged in horrific human rights abuses, called on Sunday for strong powers to pursue his probe.
Ettore Gallo, a former president of Italy's Constitutional Court, said it was vital that his five-member commission should enjoy powers similar to those of the judiciary.

He said the commission, which includes two generals and two women, would meet for the first time on Monday to discuss allegations, made in the news magazine Panorama, of torture, sexual assault and killings of Somalis by Italian peace-keepers.
"We should be conferred the same powers as judicial authorities," Gallo told La Repubblica newspaper.
"If we invite someone to hear his version of events and that person refuses to cooperate, the matter would be over before it had started. What are we meant to do without any powers?" he asked.

Prime Minister Romano Prodi ordered the inquiry last Friday after Panorama followed up previous allegations of torture by Italian troops in Somalia with photographs of soldiers seemingly assaulting a semi-naked woman tied to an armoured car.
The allegations, accompanied by interviews with Italian soldiers who served on the multinational Somalia mission from late 1992 to early 1994, have caused profound shock in Italy.

They coincide with Italian leadership of a multinational security force deployed in Albania and have dented a popular image among Italians of their soldiers as "brava gente" (fine people) engaged in selfless humanitarian work abroad.
Prodi told reporters on Sunday that the Gallo commission was expected to complete its work in "a very few months".

He welcomed the resignation from the army on Saturday of two officers who had commanded Italian forces in Somalia, generals Bruno Loi and Carmine Fiore, saying their gesture demonstrated willingness within the armed forces to get to the truth.
"With our commission, we want to identify who was responsible but we also want to safeguard the honour and good name of those who have served their country," he said.
Gallo, 73, was himself tortured in World War Two by Nazi German SS forces.
One of the two women on the panel, ex-minister Tina Anselmi, is a former wartime partisan. The other woman, Tullia Zevi, is head of Italy's Jewish Communities.
An internal armed forces inquiry and a military prosecutor's investigation are also being held into the actions of Italian troops in Somalia, a former Italian colony.
Investigations are also under way in Canada and Belgium following accusations of atrocities by their soldiers.

In Italy, one non-commissioned officer identified from the Panorama photographs has already been suspended from duty, and television on Sunday said military prosecutor Antonino Intelisano had identified a second soldier. It gave no details.
The scandal has prompted calls from some political parties, particularly on the left, for the disbanding of Italy's elite Folgore paratroop division, which served in Somalia.
Fausto Bertinotti, leader of the hard-left Communist Refoundation party, also called on Sunday for President Oscar Luigi Scalfaro to apologise to the people of Somalia.
